---

As I stood shivering in the frost of a bleak winter's night,
I was startled by a sudden warmth that set my heart alight.
Lifting a wary gaze to seek the source of this strange fire,
I beheld a radiant Child suspended in the air entire—
A Babe ablaze with heavenly flame, who wept such burning tears
As if to quench the very fire that fed his tender years.

"Alas," he spoke, "though newly born, I burn with searing pain,
Yet none draw near to share my warmth or feel this fiery strain.
My innocent breast becomes the forge; sharp thorns supply the fuel;
Love kindles the flame, and sighs rise as smoke, while shame and scorn are its cruel
Remains. Justice lays the kindling, Mercy fans the glowing coals,
And in this furnace are refined the tarnished hearts of men's souls.
For this I now am set ablaze, to labor for their good,
And I shall melt into a healing bath to cleanse them in my blood."

With these words, he vanished swiftly from my sight,
And I remembered then—it was Christmas night.

---

On a bitterly cold winter evening, I found myself trembling amid falling snow, when unexpectedly a burst of warmth caught me off guard, causing my chest to fill with glowing heat. Startled, I raised my eyes anxiously to discover the source of this blaze, and there, suspended in the air, appeared a beautiful infant wrapped in brilliant flames. Tormented by the intense heat, the child wept so profusely that the tears seemed intended to douse the very fire that fed upon them.

“How sorrowful,” the infant spoke, “I have only just come into existence, yet already I burn in these consuming flames, and not a single soul draws near to warm themselves or share in my fire besides myself. This innocent chest of mine serves as the forge, and piercing thorns are what feeds its flames. Passion itself is the blaze, my sighs rise like smoke, while disgrace and mockery settle as the remaining embers. Righteousness supplies the kindling, and Compassion stirs the burning coals. Within this forge, it is the tainted souls of humanity that are being refined. I endure these flames now so that I might bring them to salvation, and eventually, I shall dissolve into a cleansing pool, bathing them in my own blood.”

With these words, the vision disappeared instantly, fading from view, and it was then I suddenly remembered—this was the night of Christmas.

# The Burning Babe

The night pressed close and bitter, one of those deep winter evenings when the cold seems to seep not merely into flesh but into the very marrow of thought. I had gone out beneath a sky scoured clean of clouds, my breath rising in pale clouds before me, my limbs stiffened against the frost that silvered every blade of grass and every bare branch. The world seemed locked in ice, still and silent, as though even time itself had grown numb.

It was then, without warning, that I felt a sudden warmth—an impossible heat that seemed to bloom from nowhere, contradicting the frozen air around me. Startled, I looked up, and there, suspended in the darkness, I beheld a most astonishing sight: a small child, an infant newly formed, wreathed entirely in flame. He hung in the air as though cradled by unseen arms, his tiny form glowing like a coal drawn fresh from the hearth, radiant and terrible in equal measure.

The Babe wept. Great tears coursed down his small cheeks, provoked by the very fire that enveloped him, as though the heat of his own burning were more than his infant frame could bear. Yet for all his weeping, the flames did not diminish. His tears, which might have quenched any ordinary blaze, fell uselessly against a fire that burned by some other law than nature's own—a fire that fed on something other than wood or oil, something that no water could touch.

Through his tears, the child spoke, and his voice carried a sorrow too vast for his tiny frame. He lamented that though he had only just come into being—new to the world, scarcely born—he alone among all creatures was made to suffer this burning. No other soul stirred to share his torment; no hand reached out to comfort him; no heart burned alongside his in sympathy. He was solitary in his fire, newly arrived yet already marked for suffering, already set apart to bear alone what no other being would bear with him.

Then, still weeping, the Babe began to unfold the meaning of his own torment, speaking as though his suffering were not senseless but purposeful, wrought with deliberate design. His innocent breast, he explained, was no mere breast at all, but a furnace—a forge built for refining. The love that filled him, pure and unquenchable, was the very fire that fed the flames. His sighs, each one wrung from him by anguish, rose like smoke from that furnace, visible signs of the invisible burning within. And the souls of men—sinful, corrupted, in need of purification—were the metal cast into that fire, the base ore that needed such heat to be refined into something worthy.

He, the Babe declared, would be consumed so that others might be cleansed. His fire was not senseless torment but sacrifice, not cruelty but love's own instrument. He spoke further, promising that this burning was but a prelude—that he would yet melt entirely, dissolving into a bath of his own blood, and that in this final dissolution, the stain upon human souls would be washed away. His suffering, begun in fire, would end in blood, and through both fire and blood, mankind would find its cleansing.

No sooner had he spoken these words than the vision faded, the burning child dissolving back into the dark winter air as swiftly and silently as he had appeared. The warmth that had so startled me vanished with him, and the cold rushed back to claim the night, as though nothing at all had disturbed its frozen stillness.

Yet I remained transfixed, understanding then what I had witnessed. It came to me suddenly, with the force of revelation, that this was no idle dream nor wandering fancy of an overtired mind, but a vision granted on this night of all nights—for it was Christmas Day. The burning Babe was no ordinary child, but a sign and symbol of that greater Child whose birth the season commemorated: one born into suffering, marked from his very first moment for a fire that would not be quenched, a love that would consume him utterly, and a sacrifice that would, in time, cleanse the world entire.
outputs.L4:
# The Burning Babe

*A meditation on the Nativity*

The night was cold, and cruel winter's frost
Had crept upon the fields and hollow ground,
When I, alone, my careless steps had lost,
And wandered forth where snow lay all around.
My limbs were numbed, my very heart grew chill,
As I stood shivering on that lonely hill.

Then suddenly, as I looked up in fear,
A strange and dazzling brightness pierced the night—
Not from the moon, nor stars that shine so clear,
But from a sudden, unexpected light
That hovered near, and as I gazed, behold,
A tiny infant, wrapped in fire untold.

He hung suspended in the frozen air,
His small form wrapped in flames that licked and burned,
Yet from his eyes there fell, in anguished care,
Great scalding tears, as if his heart had yearned
To weep for sorrows that no words could tell—
A living furnace, yet a fountain as well.

"Alas!" I cried, "What means this fearful sight?
A babe on fire, yet weeping bitter tears?
Pray tell me, wondrous vision of the night,
What mystery is this that so appears?"
The infant then, with voice both soft and mild,
Spoke thus to me, though but a newborn child:

"My faultless breast the furnace is," he said,
"The fuel wounding thorns, for which I burn;
For Love the fire is kindled, and I'm fed
By sighs and groans that in my bosom churn.
Justice provides the coals in scorching heat,
With mercy blown, to make the flame complete.

"And in this furnace I must melt and prove
The dross of sin that stains the human soul;
So many souls that wander far from love,
So many hearts that Satan doth control.
For them I burn, for them these tears I shed,
That they might live, though I be counted dead.

"This fire shall not consume, but shall refine
The gold of grace within the human breast;
My tears shall wash away the stain of time,
And bring the weary, sinful soul to rest.
Though now an infant, small and weak I seem,
Yet from this fire shall rise redemption's gleam.

"For I must grow, and walk upon the earth,
And bear the cross that men have made for me;
This burning now foretells my humble birth
Shall lead at last unto Golgotha's tree.
There shall my blood, more precious than this flame,
Wash clean the world and cleanse it of its shame."

With that, the vision faded from my sight,
The flames grew dim, the infant disappeared,
And I was left alone in winter's night,
My mind confounded, yet my spirit cheered.
I looked about, bewildered by the scene,
And wondered what this vision all could mean.

Then did I recollect, with sudden start,
The very day and season I stood in—
'Twas Christmas morn! And with a leaping heart,
I understood the vision's origin:
For on this day, the Christ-child came to earth,
To bring, through fire and tears, our souls new birth.

The burning babe I saw was but a sign
Of that great love which knows no earthly bound,
Which came to dwell in flesh, both his and mine,
And in our winter's cold, warm mercy found.
So let us mark this day with joyful praise,
For in this Child, our hope forever stays.

---

*Thus doth the poet's vision, strange and bright,*
*Reveal the mystery of that holy morn,*
*When God took flesh to conquer sin's dark night,*
*And Love itself as helpless babe was born—*
*A fire that warms, yet burns away all wrong,*
*A tale of grace, retold in Christmas song.*
outputs.L5:
# Surprise, Babe

The kitchen was dark when she walked in, and for a moment she thought maybe she'd forgotten to pay the electric bill again. Then the lights flicked on, and there he was, standing next to a cake with too many candles and a grin that made her forget she'd had a terrible day.

"Surprise, babe," he said, and somehow those two words undid every knot of stress she'd carried in from work.

She laughed, half in disbelief, half in that warm rush of being truly seen. It wasn't her birthday. It wasn't any occasion she could name. But that was exactly the point—he didn't need a reason. He'd just wanted to remind her that she mattered, that ordinary Tuesdays could hold something extraordinary if you paid enough attention.

The cake was slightly lopsided, clearly homemade, with frosting that suggested more enthusiasm than skill. It didn't matter. What mattered was the effort behind it, the thought that had gone into remembering she'd mentioned loving lemon cake three weeks ago in passing conversation, the fact that he'd cleared his evening just to see her face light up.

"You didn't have to do this," she said, setting down her bag.

"I know," he replied. "I wanted to."

Sometimes love isn't about grand gestures or perfect timing. Sometimes it's just someone saying *surprise, babe* on a random Tuesday, turning an unremarkable evening into something you'll remember for years. It's in the small rebellions against routine, the tiny acts that say *I see you, I thought of you, you are worth celebrating* even when there's no calendar date demanding it.

She blew out the candles anyway, made a wish she didn't need, and reached for his hand instead of a fork.
